claim: Amyloid β (Aβ) peptides accumulating in the brain are proposed to trigger Alzheimer's disease (AD).
source: Amyloid β (Aβ) peptides accumulating in the brain are proposed to trigger Alzheimer's disease (AD).
evidence: This is a well-established hypothesis in the field, supported by citation to the broader literature.

claim: Molecular cascades underlying Aβ toxicity are poorly defined.
source: However, molecular cascades underlying their toxicity are poorly defined.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Human Aβ42 peptides inhibit γ-secretases.
source: We show that human Aβ42 peptides, but neither murine Aβ42 nor human Aβ17–42 (p3), inhibit γ-secretases and trigger accumulation of unprocessed substrates in neurons, including C-terminal fragments (CTFs) of APP, p75, and pan-cadherin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including cell-free assays and cellular experiments.

claim: Murine Aβ42 does not inhibit γ-secretases.
source: We show that human Aβ42 peptides, but neither murine Aβ42 nor human Aβ17–42 (p3), inhibit γ-secretases and trigger accumulation of unprocessed substrates in neurons, including C-terminal fragments (CTFs) of APP, p75, and pan-cadherin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing human and murine Aβ42 in cell-free and cellular assays.

claim: Human Aβ17–42 (p3) does not inhibit γ-secretases.
source: We show that human Aβ42 peptides, but neither murine Aβ42 nor human Aβ17–42 (p3), inhibit γ-secretases and trigger accumulation of unprocessed substrates in neurons, including C-terminal fragments (CTFs) of APP, p75, and pan-cadherin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing human Aβ42 and p3 in cell-free and cellular assays.

claim: Human Aβ42 triggers accumulation of unprocessed substrates in neurons, including C-terminal fragments (CTFs) of APP, p75, and pan-cadherin.
source: We show that human Aβ42 peptides, but neither murine Aβ42 nor human Aβ17–42 (p3), inhibit γ-secretases and trigger accumulation of unprocessed substrates in neurons, including C-terminal fragments (CTFs) of APP, p75, and pan-cadherin.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data from neuronal cell lines and human neurons.

claim: Aβ42 treatment dysregulated cellular homeostasis, as shown by the induction of p75-dependent neuronal death in two distinct cellular systems.
source: Moreover, Aβ42 treatment dysregulated cellular homeostasis, as shown by the induction of p75-dependent neuronal death in two distinct cellular systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemical analysis of cleaved caspase 3 in PC12nnr5 cells and basal forebrain cholinergic neurons.

claim: Pathological elevations in Aβ42 may contribute to cellular toxicity via γ-secretase inhibition.
source: Our findings raise the possibility that pathological elevations in Aβ42 contribute to cellular toxicity via the γ-secretase inhibition, and provide a novel conceptual framework to address Aβ toxicity in the context of γ-secretase-dependent homeostatic signaling.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Aberrant processing of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) by γ-secretases leads to the production of longer, aggregation-prone Aβ peptides that contribute to neurodegeneration.
source: Aberrant processing of the amyloid precursor protein (APP) by γ-secretases leads to the production of longer, aggregation-prone Aβ peptides that contribute to neurodegeneration (Selkoe and Hardy, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Selkoe and Hardy, 2016.

claim: γ-secretases process many membrane proteins, including NOTCH, ERB-B2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 (ERBB4), N-cadherin (NCAD), and p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75-NTR).
source: In addition, γ-secretases process many other membrane proteins, including NOTCH, ERB-B2 receptor tyrosine kinase 4 (ERBB4), N-cadherin (NCAD), and p75 neurotrophin receptor (p75-NTR) (Haapasalo and Kovacs, 2011; Güner and Lichtenthaler, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haapasalo and Kovacs, 2011 and Güner and Lichtenthaler, 2020.

claim: Treatments with γ-secretase inhibitors caused cognitive worsening in AD patients.
source: It is noteworthy that treatments with γ-secretase inhibitors caused cognitive worsening in AD patients (Doody et al., 2013), while full genetic inhibition of these enzymes in the adult mouse brain led to neurodegenerative phenotypes (Acx et al., 2017; Wines-Samuelson et al., 2010; Tabuchi et al., 2009; Saura et al., 2004; Bi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Doody et al., 2013.

claim: Full genetic inhibition of γ-secretases in the adult mouse brain led to neurodegenerative phenotypes.
source: It is noteworthy that treatments with γ-secretase inhibitors caused cognitive worsening in AD patients (Doody et al., 2013), while full genetic inhibition of these enzymes in the adult mouse brain led to neurodegenerative phenotypes (Acx et al., 2017; Wines-Samuelson et al., 2010; Tabuchi et al., 2009; Saura et al., 2004; Bi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Acx et al., 2017; Wines-Samuelson et al., 2010; Tabuchi et al., 2009; Saura et al., 2004; Bi et al., 2021.

claim: The proteolytic activities of γ-secretase complexes are promoted by the low pH of the endosomal and lysosomal compartments.
source: The proteolytic activities of these complexes are promoted by the low pH of the endosomal and lysosomal compartments, wherein the amyloidogenic processing of APP occurs (Maesako et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maesako et al., 2022.

claim: In the amyloidogenic pathway, the proteolytic processing of APP by β-secretase (BACE) releases a soluble APP ectodomain and generates a membrane-bound C-terminal fragment (β-CTF or APPC99).
source: In the amyloidogenic pathway, the proteolytic processing of APP by β-secretase (BACE) releases a soluble APP ectodomain and generates a membrane-bound C-terminal fragment (β-CTF or APPC99) (Vassar et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vassar et al., 1999.

claim: APPC99 is sequentially processed within the membrane by γ-secretase complexes.
source: APPC99 is then sequentially processed within the membrane by γ-secretase complexes (Figure 1A; Takami et al., 2009; Bolduc et al., 2016; Chávez-Gutiérrez et al., 2012; Qi-Takahara et al., 2005; Funamoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Takami et al., 2009; Bolduc et al., 2016; Chávez-Gutiérrez et al., 2012; Qi-Takahara et al., 2005; Funamoto et al., 2004, and by Figure 1A.

claim: An initial endopeptidase (ε-) cut releases the APP intracellular domain (AICD) into the cytosol and generates a de novo substrate (either Aβ49 or Aβ48 peptide) that undergoes successive γ-cleavages until a shortened Aβ peptide can be released into the luminal or extracellular environment.
source: An initial endopeptidase (ε-) cut releases the APP intracellular domain (AICD) into the cytosol and generates a de novo substrate (either Aβ49 or Aβ48 peptide) that undergoes successive γ-cleavages until a shortened Aβ peptide can be released into the luminal or extracellular environment.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of γ-secretase processing of APP.

claim: The efficiency of the sequential cleavage mechanism (i.e. processivity) determines the length of Aβ (37–43 amino acid long peptides), which in turn influences the aggregation and neurotoxic properties of the peptides produced.
source: The efficiency of the sequential cleavage mechanism (i.e. processivity) determines the length of Aβ (37–43 amino acid long peptides), which in turn influences the aggregation and neurotoxic properties of the peptides produced (Selkoe and Hardy, 2016; Kakuda et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Selkoe and Hardy, 2016; Kakuda et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2017.

claim: In the non-amyloidogenic pathway APP is cleaved by α- and γ-secretases to generate a spectrum of p3 peptides, which lack the first 1–16 amino acids of Aβ.
source: In the non-amyloidogenic pathway APP is cleaved by α- and γ-secretases to generate a spectrum of p3 peptides, which lack the first 1–16 amino acids of Aβ (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the established non-amyloidogenic pathway and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: p3 peptides are not linked to AD pathogenesis.
source: Despite their relatively high hydrophobicity and aggregation-prone behavior, the p3 peptides are not linked to AD pathogenesis (Kuhn and Raskatov, 2020; Lichtenthaler, 2011; Tambini et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kuhn and Raskatov, 2020; Lichtenthaler, 2011; Tambini et al., 2020.

claim: Mutations that promote the amyloidogenic processing of APP are associated with AD.
source: In fact, mutations that promote the amyloidogenic processing of APP are associated with AD (Mullan et al., 1992; Pagnon de la Vega et al., 2021), whereas those that favor the alternative, non-amyloidogenic pathway protect against the disease (Tambini et al., 2020; Jansen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mullan et al., 1992; Pagnon de la Vega et al., 2021.

claim: Mutations that favor the alternative, non-amyloidogenic pathway protect against AD.
source: In fact, mutations that promote the amyloidogenic processing of APP are associated with AD (Mullan et al., 1992; Pagnon de la Vega et al., 2021), whereas those that favor the alternative, non-amyloidogenic pathway protect against the disease (Tambini et al., 2020; Jansen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tambini et al., 2020; Jansen et al., 2019.

claim: Human Aβ42 inhibits γ-secretase-mediated proteolysis of APPC99 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The analysis demonstrated that human Aβ42 inhibited γ-secretase-mediated proteolysis of APPC99 in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The IC50 for human Aβ42 inhibition of γ-secretase is 1.3 μM at 0.4 μM APPC99 substrate concentration.
source: The more pronounced peptide-driven inhibition at the lower substrate concentration (IC50=1.3 μM vs 3.6 μM for 0.4 and 1.2 μM APPC99, respectively) is consistent with a mechanism in which Aβ42 competes with the substrate for the enzyme.
evidence: This IC50 value is derived from the dose-response data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The IC50 for human Aβ42 inhibition of γ-secretase is 3.6 μM at 1.2 μM APPC99 substrate concentration.
source: The more pronounced peptide-driven inhibition at the lower substrate concentration (IC50=1.3 μM vs 3.6 μM for 0.4 and 1.2 μM APPC99, respectively) is consistent with a mechanism in which Aβ42 competes with the substrate for the enzyme.
evidence: This IC50 value is derived from the dose-response data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Aβ42 competes with the substrate for the enzyme.
source: The more pronounced peptide-driven inhibition at the lower substrate concentration (IC50=1.3 μM vs 3.6 μM for 0.4 and 1.2 μM APPC99, respectively) is consistent with a mechanism in which Aβ42 competes with the substrate for the enzyme.
evidence: This is an inference based on the substrate concentration-dependent IC50 values.

claim: Aβ42 partially inhibited the generation of both AICD product types (AICD50-99 and AICD49-99).
source: In addition, mass spectrometry analyses of the proteolytic reactions showed that Aβ42 partially inhibited the generation of both AICD product types (AICD50-99 and AICD49-99) (Figure 1C), indicating that Aβ42 inhibits both γ-secretase product lines.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Aβ42 inhibits both γ-secretase product lines.
source: In addition, mass spectrometry analyses of the proteolytic reactions showed that Aβ42 partially inhibited the generation of both AICD product types (AICD50-99 and AICD49-99) (Figure 1C), indicating that Aβ42 inhibits both γ-secretase product lines.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mass spectrometry data showing inhibition of both AICD product types.

claim: Human Aβ42 exerted inhibition on all members of the γ-secretase family – i.e., irrespective of the type of PSEN (1 vs 2) and APH1 (A vs B) subunits.
source: Quantitative western blotting analysis revealed a marked inhibition of total AICD production by all types of γ-secretases in the presence of 3 µM human Aβ42.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Despite the use of relatively high concentrations of Aβ42 (10 µM), this peptide was not converted into Aβ38.
source: Despite the use of relatively high concentrations of Aβ42 (10 µM), this peptide was not converted into Aβ38.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Proteolytic reactions using APPC99 (1.5 μM) resulted in the generation of Aβ38 (0.5–1 nM).
source: In contrast, proteolytic reactions using APPC99 (1.5 μM) resulted in the generation of Aβ38 (0.5–1 nM).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Aβ42 was barely converted into Aβ38 in detergent-resistant membranes (DRMs).
source: As in the detergent conditions, Aβ42 was barely converted into Aβ38.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: γ-secretase processes Aβ43 into Aβ40 under similar conditions, even when this peptide was added at much lower concentrations (0.5–1 µM).
source: We note that γ-secretase processes Aβ43 into Aβ40 under similar conditions, even when this peptide was added at much lower concentrations (0.5–1 µM) (Szaruga et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szaruga et al., 2017.

claim: Exogenous Aβ42 does interact with γ-secretases but does not act as a substrate.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that exogenous Aβ42 does interact with γ-secretases but, unlike Aβ43, does not act as a substrate (at least under these conditions), supporting the notion that Aβ42-driven inhibition of γ-secretases is mediated via the formation of non-productive enzyme-substrate (E-S) like complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ42 is not processed to Aβ38 but does inhibit γ-secretase.

claim: Aβ42-driven inhibition of γ-secretases is mediated via the formation of non-productive enzyme-substrate (E-S) like complexes.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate that exogenous Aβ42 does interact with γ-secretases but, unlike Aβ43, does not act as a substrate (at least under these conditions), supporting the notion that Aβ42-driven inhibition of γ-secretases is mediated via the formation of non-productive enzyme-substrate (E-S) like complexes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ42 inhibits γ-secretase but is not processed.

claim: Aβ42 inhibition of γ-secretase is fully reversible.
source: Analysis of the levels of the de novo generated AICD products in the supernatant fractions collected before (reaction 1) and after washes (reaction 2) indicated that Aβ42 inhibition of γ-secretase is fully reversible (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Aβ42 forms a non-productive E-S-like complex with γ-secretase and its binding is reversible.
source: Collectively, our analyses support a model wherein Aβ42 forms a non-productive E-S-like complex with γ-secretase and its binding is reversible.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the reversibility data and the observation that Aβ42 is not processed.

claim: Murine Aβ42 maximally inhibited γ-secretase activity by ~20%.
source: Quantification of the de novo AICD product levels showed that murine Aβ42 maximally inhibited γ-secretase activity by ~20% (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Three amino acids in the N-terminal domain (R5G, Y10F and H13R) differentiate human and murine Aβ1–42 peptides.
source: As three amino acids in the N-terminal domain (R5G, Y10F and H13R) differentiate human and murine Aβ1–42 peptides (Figure 1A), the differences in the inhibition thus defined the N-terminal domain of Aβ as contributing to the inhibitory mechanism.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The N-terminal domain of Aβ contributes to the inhibitory mechanism.
source: As three amino acids in the N-terminal domain (R5G, Y10F and H13R) differentiate human and murine Aβ1–42 peptides (Figure 1A), the differences in the inhibition thus defined the N-terminal domain of Aβ as contributing to the inhibitory mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential inhibitory potencies of human and murine Aβ42.

claim: Similar to human Aβ1–42, murine Aβ1–42 was not processed to Aβ1–38.
source: It is noteworthy that similar to human Aβ1–42, murine Aβ1–42 was not processed to Aβ1–38 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The IC50 values for Aβ11–42 were reduced 1.79- and 1.31-fold (KM and saturating substrate concentrations, respectively), relative to Aβ42.
source: The IC50 values for Aβ11–42 were reduced 1.79- and 1.31-fold (KM and saturating substrate concentrations, respectively), relative to Aβ42 (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1a), while the larger N-terminal truncation (of residues 1–16) even further reduced the inhibitory effect to the level seen with murine Aβ42 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1a.

claim: The larger N-terminal truncation (of residues 1–16) even further reduced the inhibitory effect to the level seen with murine Aβ42.
source: The IC50 values for Aβ11–42 were reduced 1.79- and 1.31-fold (KM and saturating substrate concentrations, respectively), relative to Aβ42 (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1a), while the larger N-terminal truncation (of residues 1–16) even further reduced the inhibitory effect to the level seen with murine Aβ42 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The N-terminal region of Aβ plays a defining role in the inhibition of γ-secretase activity.
source: Collectively, these data assign a defining role to the N-terminal region of Aβ in the inhibition of γ-secretase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure-function analysis of N-terminally truncated Aβ peptides.

claim: Relative to Aβ42, shorter Aβ species exerted progressively less or no inhibition on the de novo generation of AICD.
source: Relative to Aβ42, shorter Aβ species exerted progressively less or no inhibition on the de novo generation of AICD.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Peptides longer than Aβ42 serve as substrates for γ-secretases under these conditions.
source: It is noteworthy that peptides longer than Aβ42 serve as substrates for γ-secretases under these conditions, and their shortening potentially converts them into less potent inhibitory species (Szaruga et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szaruga et al., 2017.

claim: Both Aβ C- and N-termini modulate the inhibitory mechanism.
source: Taken together, these data strengthen the conclusion that human Aβ42 inhibits γ-secretases and indicate that both Aβ C- and N-termini modulate the inhibitory mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure-function analysis of various Aβ peptides.

claim: Human Aβ42 treatment increased the APP-CTF/FL ratio in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: Human Aβ42 treatment increased the APP-CTF/FL ratio, a read-out of γ-secretase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Treatment with p3 peptide had no effect on the APP-CTF/FL ratio.
source: In contrast, treatment with p3 peptide had no effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was a ~50% reduction in luminescence signal, directly linked to HiBiT-Aβ levels, in CM of cells treated with human Aβ42.
source: We found a ~50% reduction in luminescence signal, directly linked to HiBiT-Aβ levels, in CM of cells treated with human Aβ42 and no effect of p3 peptide treatment, relative to the DMSO control (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by luminescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was no effect of p3 peptide treatment on HiBiT-Aβ levels, relative to the DMSO control.
source: We found a ~50% reduction in luminescence signal, directly linked to HiBiT-Aβ levels, in CM of cells treated with human Aβ42 and no effect of p3 peptide treatment, relative to the DMSO control (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by luminescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The observed reduction in the total Aβ products is consistent with the partial inhibition of γ-secretase by Aβ42.
source: The observed reduction in the total Aβ products is consistent with the partial inhibition of γ-secretase by Aβ42.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduction in HiBiT-Aβ levels.

claim: There was no significant change in cellular toxicity measures in response to Aβ42 (1 μM), p3 17–42 (1 μM) or GSI (2 μM).
source: There was no significant change in these measures in response to Aβ42 (1 μM), p3 17–42 (1 μM) or GSI (2 μM) (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATP-based viability assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Only treatment with human Aβ42 resulted in a significant increase of APP-CTFs in iPSC-derived neurons.
source: Only treatment with human Aβ42 resulted in a significant increase of APP-CTFs (Figure 3H), supporting the inhibitory role of Aβ42.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Only human Aβ42 significantly increased the APP-CTF/FL ratio in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: The analysis confirmed a significant ~2.5 fold increase in the APP-CTF/APP-FL ratio in cells treated with human Aβ42 but, intriguingly, none of the other investigated peptides significantly changed APP-CTF levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: None of the other investigated peptides significantly changed APP-CTF levels in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: The analysis confirmed a significant ~2.5 fold increase in the APP-CTF/APP-FL ratio in cells treated with human Aβ42 but, intriguingly, none of the other investigated peptides significantly changed APP-CTF levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Selective cellular uptake of human Aβ42, relative to Aβ40, leads to its concentration in the acidic endolysosomal network (ELN), promoting peptide aggregation into soluble toxic Aβ species.
source: Previous studies have shown that selective cellular uptake of human Aβ42, relative to Aβ40, leading to its concentration in the acidic endolysosomal network (ELN), promotes peptide aggregation into soluble toxic Aβ species (Hu et al., 2009; Su and Chang, 2001; Schützmann et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2010; Esbjörner et al., 2014; Friedrich et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2009; Su and Chang, 2001; Schützmann et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2010; Esbjörner et al., 2014; Friedrich et al., 2010.

claim: Unlike other Aβ or p3 peptides, human Aβ42 accumulated in PC12 cells.
source: We found that, unlike other Aβ or p3 peptides, human Aβ42 accumulated in cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The pattern of Aβ42 accumulation appeared distinct, punctate, and largely perinuclear, suggestive of its presence in the endolysosomal compartment.
source: The pattern of the accumulation appeared distinct, punctate, and largely perinuclear, suggestive of its presence in the endolysosomal compartment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the immunostaining pattern shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Intracellular accumulation of Aβ42 distinguishes it from the other peptides studied and explains its apparently unique inhibitory properties in the cellular context.
source: The data are consistent with a model in which intracellular accumulation of Aβ42, due to a selective cellular uptake or reduced peptide degradation, distinguishes it from the other peptides studied and explains its apparently unique inhibitory properties in the cellular context.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the differential cellular accumulation and inhibitory properties of Aβ42.

claim: Significant increases in FRET efficiency in cells treated with human Aβ42 or GSI, relative to vehicle-treated cultures, indicated increments in the levels of the full-length (uncleaved) fluorescent substrate, and thus reduced γ-secretase activity.
source: While p3 peptides did not affect the FRET signal, significant increases in FRET efficiency (i.e. increased proximity between YPet and Turquoise-GL) in cells treated with human Aβ42 or GSI, relative to vehicle-treated cultures, indicated increments in the levels of the full-length (uncleaved) fluorescent substrate, and thus reduced γ-secretase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: p3 peptides did not affect the FRET signal in mouse primary neurons.
source: While p3 peptides did not affect the FRET signal, significant increases in FRET efficiency (i.e. increased proximity between YPet and Turquoise-GL) in cells treated with human Aβ42 or GSI, relative to vehicle-treated cultures, indicated increments in the levels of the full-length (uncleaved) fluorescent substrate, and thus reduced γ-secretase activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: There was no evidence of increased either α-secretase or β-secretase levels in SH-SY5Y cells treated with Aβ42.
source: We found no evidence of increased either α-secretase or β-secretase levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a reduction in total sAPP levels in the conditioned medium collected from cells treated with Aβ42.
source: Our analysis showed a reduction in total sAPP levels in the conditioned medium collected from cells treated with Aβ42.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decrease in total sAPP is inconsistent with an Aβ42-mediated effect that would increase APP-CTF levels as a result of activating α-secretase or β-secretase activity.
source: This finding is inconsistent with an Aβ42-mediated effect that would increase APP-CTF levels as a result of activating α-secretase or β-secretase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that sAPP levels decreased rather than increased.

claim: Bafilomycin A1 treatment markedly prolonged the half-life of both APP-CTFs and APP-FL.
source: Quantitative analysis of the levels of both APP-CTFs and APP-FL over the 5 h time-course showed that bafilomycin A1 treatment markedly prolonged the half-life of both proteins but did not reveal significant differences in their levels between GSI versus GSI plus Aβ42-treated cells (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: There were no significant differences in APP-CTF and APP-FL levels between GSI versus GSI plus Aβ42-treated cells over the 5 h time-course.
source: Quantitative analysis of the levels of both APP-CTFs and APP-FL over the 5 h time-course showed that bafilomycin A1 treatment markedly prolonged the half-life of both proteins but did not reveal significant differences in their levels between GSI versus GSI plus Aβ42-treated cells (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: The lack of significant effects of Aβ42 on the levels of APP-CTFs under conditions of full γ-secretase inhibition suggests that the peptide does not induce major defects in cellular degradation pathways, at least at this concentration.
source: The lack of a significant effects of Aβ42 on the levels of APP-CTFs under these conditions (full γ-secretase inhibition) suggests that the peptide does not induce major defects in cellular degradation pathways, at least at this concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cycloheximide chase data.

claim: There was an increased APP-CTF/FL ratio in GSI + Aβ42 treated cells vs GSI + DMSO treated ones at time zero.
source: However, we noted an increased APP-CTF/FL ratio in GSI + Aβ42 treated cells vs GSI + DMSO treated ones at time zero (Figure 6D), suggesting that the Aβ42-induced increase in APP-CTFs is mediated by both inhibition of γ-secretase and one or more additional mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The Aβ42-induced increase in APP-CTFs is mediated by both inhibition of γ-secretase and one or more additional mechanisms.
source: However, we noted an increased APP-CTF/FL ratio in GSI + Aβ42 treated cells vs GSI + DMSO treated ones at time zero (Figure 6D), suggesting that the Aβ42-induced increase in APP-CTFs is mediated by both inhibition of γ-secretase and one or more additional mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ42 increases APP-CTF/FL ratio even in the presence of GSI.

claim: Aβ42-mediated γ-secretase inhibition plays a more prominent role than other mechanisms in APP-CTF accumulation.
source: Nevertheless, the greater relative accumulation of APP-CTFs in the absence (138%) (Figure 3A) versus the presence (48%) of the GSI (Figure 6D) is evidence that Aβ42-mediated γ-secretase inhibition plays a more prominent role.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the magnitude of APP-CTF accumulation with and without GSI.

claim: Significant increments in the APP-CTF/FL ratio were observed in cells treated with SWE-conditioned media, relative to control cells.
source: We observed significant increments in the APP-CTF/FL ratio in cells treated with SWE-conditioned media, relative to control cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Aβ immunodepletion from the SWE medium (delSWE-CM) lowered the APP-CTF/FL ratio to the levels observed in the control cells.
source: Aβ immunodepletion from the SWE medium (delSWE-CM) lowered the APP-CTF/FL ratio to the levels observed in the control cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Aβ peptides derived from biological sources induce the accumulation of APP-CTFs even when present at low nM concentrations.
source: These data provide evidence that Aβ peptides derived from biological sources induce the accumulation of APP-CTFs even when present at low nM concentrations, and thus point to this biological source of Aβ as being far more potent than the recombinant Aβ42.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that conditioned medium with low nM Aβ induces APP-CTF accumulation.

claim: Human Aβ42 inhibited γ-secretase-mediated processing of NOTCH1 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Quantification of the de novo generated NICD-3xFLAG showed a dose-dependent inhibition of γ-secretase proteolysis of NOTCH1 by Aβ42.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The degree of inhibition of NOTCH1 processing by Aβ42 depended on substrate concentration, consistent with a competitive mechanism.
source: As for APPC99, the derived IC50 values showed that the degree of the inhibition depended on substrate concentration, consistent with a competitive mechanism (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is an inference based on the substrate concentration-dependent IC50 values.

claim: Aβ42 reduced γ-secretase proteolysis of ERBB4-, neurexin-, and p75-based substrates.
source: Quantification of the respective de novo generated ICDs revealed that Aβ42 reduced γ-secretase proteolysis of each of these substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Treatment with human Aβ42 and InhX, but not p3, resulted in significant increases in the PanCad-CTF/FL ratio.
source: Treatment with human Aβ42 and InhX, but not p3, resulted in significant increases in the PanCad-CTF/FL ratio, demonstrating that Aβ42 inhibits the processing of several different γ-secretase substrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Aβ42 inhibits the processing of several different γ-secretase substrates.
source: Treatment with human Aβ42 and InhX, but not p3, resulted in significant increases in the PanCad-CTF/FL ratio, demonstrating that Aβ42 inhibits the processing of several different γ-secretase substrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ42 increases CTF/FL ratios for multiple substrates.

claim: A ~20% significant reduction in the amount of secreted N-terminal HiBiT-tagged peptides derived from the NOTCH1-based substrates in cells treated with Aβ1–42 supports the inhibitory action of Aβ1–42 on γ-secretase mediated proteolysis.
source: A~20% significant reduction in the amount of secreted N-terminal HiBiT-tagged peptides derived from the NOTCH1-based substrates in cells treated with Aβ1–42 supports the inhibitory action of Aβ1–42 on γ-secretase mediated proteolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by luminescence data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Aβ42 inhibits enzyme activity independent of substrate structure.
source: By demonstrating that Aβ42 inhibits γ-secretase proteolysis of substrates that are structurally distinct from APP-CTFs, these data indicate that Aβ42 inhibits enzyme activity independent of substrate structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ42 inhibits processing of multiple structurally distinct substrates.

claim: Accumulation of p75-CTF in basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (BFCNs), due to pharmacological inhibition of γ-secretases, triggers apoptosis in a TrkA activity-dependent manner.
source: Previous studies have shown that accumulation of p75-CTF in basal forebrain cholinergic neurons (BFCNs), due to pharmacological inhibition of γ-secretases, triggers apoptosis in a TrkA activity-dependent manner (Franco et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franco et al., 2021.

claim: The proapoptotic action of p75-CTF is prevented by the expression of the TrkA receptor for nerve growth factor (NGF).
source: The proapoptotic action of p75-CTF is prevented by the expression of the TrkA receptor for nerve growth factor (NGF), which serves as a co-receptor with p75 (Franco et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Franco et al., 2021.

claim: γ-secretase inhibitors increased apoptosis in TrkA-deficient (PC12nnr5), but not in wild-type, TrkA-expressing PC12 cells.
source: In this case, γ-secretase inhibitors increased apoptosis in TrkA-deficient (PC12nnr5) (Loeb et al., 1991), but not in wild-type, TrkA-expressing cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Loeb et al., 1991.

claim: Cleaved caspase 3 staining was increased in PC12nnr5 cells treated with GSI or human Aβ42, but not in those exposed to p3 or vehicle (DMSO).
source: Cleaved caspase 3 staining was increased in PC12nnr5 cells treated with GSI or human Aβ42, but not in those exposed to p3 or vehicle (DMSO).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: None of the treatments elicited significant increases in cleaved caspase 3 in wild-type PC12 cells that express physiological levels of TrkA.
source: Of note, and consistent with our previous findings (Franco et al., 2021), none of the treatments elicited significant increases in cleaved caspase 3 in wild-type PC12 cells that express physiological levels of TrkA.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 9A and citation to Franco et al., 2021.

claim: Analysis of the p75-CTF/FL ratio demonstrated higher p75-CTF levels in GSI and Aβ42 treated PC12nnr5 cells.
source: In addition, analysis of the p75-CTF/FL ratio demonstrated higher p75-CTF levels in GSI and Aβ42 treated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Aβ42-mediated accumulation of p75-CTFs results in cell death signaling in the absence or near absence of TrkA expression.
source: These results, together with our previous observations, strongly suggest that Aβ42-mediated accumulation of p75-CTFs results in cell death signaling in the absence or near absence of TrkA expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Aβ42 increases cleaved caspase 3 in TrkA-deficient cells.

claim: Treatment with 1 µM human Aβ42 mimics the increase in cleaved caspase 3 driven by the GSI in BFCNs.
source: Our similar studies using BFCNs recapitulated the reported increased cell death under conditions in which both γ-secretase and TrkA activities were inhibited (CE and K252α inhibitor) (Franco et al., 2021), and showed that treatment with 1 µM human Aβ42 mimics the increase in cleaved caspase 3 driven by the GSI (Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunocytochemical data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: An increased APP-CTF/FL ratio in Aβ42 treated synaptosomes, compared to vehicle control, provided evidence of γ-secretase inhibition.
source: An increased APP-CTF/FL ratio in Aβ42 treated samples, compared to vehicle control, provided evidence of γ-secretase inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The concentration of Aβ42 in the synaptosomes from (end-stage) AD tissues was significantly higher (10.7 nM) than those isolated from non-demented tissues (0.7 nM).
source: We observed that the concentration of Aβ42 in the synaptosomes from (end-stage) AD tissues was significantly higher (10.7 nM) than those isolated from non-demented tissues (0.7 nM), ***p<0.0005.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Endogenous Aβ42 concentrates in synaptosomes derived from end-stage AD brains to reach ~10 nM.
source: These data provide evidence for accumulation at nM concentrations of endogenous Aβ42 in synaptosomes in end-stage AD brains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ELISA measurements of Aβ42 in synaptosomes.

claim: Even higher concentrations of Aβ42 may be present in the endolysosome vesicle system within synaptosomes.
source: Given that we measured Aβ42 concentration in synaptosomes, we speculate that even higher concentrations of this peptide may be present in the endolysosome vesicle system, and therein inhibit the endogenous processing of APP-CTF at the synapse.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known localization of Aβ42 in endolysosomes.

claim: Treatment of PC12 cells with conditioned medium containing even lower amounts of Aβ (low nanomolar range (0.5–1 nM)) resulted in the accumulation of APP-CTFs.
source: Of note treatment of PC12 cells with conditioned medium containing even lower amounts of Aβ (low nanomolar range (0.5–1 nM)) resulted in the accumulation of APP-CTFs.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Increases in Aβ42 in the AD brain, and in particular in the endolysosomal compartment, facilitate the establishment of an Aβ-driven inhibitory mechanism that contributes to neurotoxicity by impairing critical γ-secretase signaling functions.
source: Collectively, our data raise the intriguing possibility that increases in Aβ42 in the AD brain, and in particular in the endolysosomal compartment, facilitate the establishment of an Aβ-driven inhibitory mechanism that contributes to neurotoxicity by impairing critical γ-secretase signaling functions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The inhibition of γ-secretase in the adult mouse brain leads to age-dependent neurodegenerative phenotypes by poorly understood but APP-independent mechanisms.
source: In this regard, we note that the inhibition of γ-secretase in the adult mouse brain leads to age-dependent neurodegenerative phenotypes (Acx et al., 2017; Wines-Samuelson et al., 2010; Tabuchi et al., 2009; Saura et al., 2004) by poorly understood but APP-independent mechanisms (Acx et al., 2017), whereas pharmacological inhibition of γ-secretase has been linked to cognitive worsening in AD affected individuals (Doody et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Acx et al., 2017; Wines-Samuelson et al., 2010; Tabuchi et al., 2009; Saura et al., 2004; Doody et al., 2013.

claim: The competitive nature of the Aβ42-mediated inhibition implies that it is partial, reversible, and regulated by the relative concentrations of the Aβ42 peptide (inhibitor) and the endogenous substrates.
source: From a mechanistic standpoint, the competitive nature of the Aβ42-mediated inhibition implies that it is partial, reversible, and regulated by the relative concentrations of the Aβ42 peptide (inhibitor) and the endogenous substrates (Figure 10C and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the competitive mechanism and reversibility data.

claim: Cellular uptake, as well as endosomal production of Aβ, result in increased intracellular concentration of Aβ42, facilitating γ-secretase inhibition and leading to the buildup of APP-CTFs (and γ-secretase substrates in general).
source: The model that we put forward is that cellular uptake, as well as endosomal production of Aβ, result in increased intracellular concentration of Aβ42, facilitating γ-secretase inhibition and leading to the buildup of APP-CTFs (and γ-secretase substrates in general).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: This cyclic inhibitory mechanism will translate into pulses of (partial) γ-secretase inhibition, which will alter γ-secretase mediated-signaling.
source: This cyclic inhibitory mechanism will translate into pulses of (partial) γ-secretase inhibition, which will alter γ-secretase mediated-signaling (arising from increased CTF levels at the membrane or decreased release of soluble intracellular domains from substrates).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the competitive and reversible nature of the inhibition.

claim: Oscillations in γ-secretase activity induced by treatment with a γ-secretase inhibitor semagacestat have been proposed to have contributed to the cognitive alterations observed in semagacestat-treated patients in the failed Phase-3 IDENTITY clinical trial.
source: It is worth noting that oscillations in γ-secretase activity induced by treatment with a γ-secretase inhibitor semagacestat have been proposed to have contributed to the cognitive alterations observed in semagacestat-treated patients in the failed Phase-3 IDENTITY clinical trial (Doody et al., 2013) and that semagacestat, like Aβ42, acts as a high affinity competitor of substrates (Koch et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Doody et al., 2013 and Koch et al., 2023.

claim: Semagacestat, like Aβ42, acts as a high affinity competitor of substrates.
source: It is worth noting that oscillations in γ-secretase activity induced by treatment with a γ-secretase inhibitor semagacestat have been proposed to have contributed to the cognitive alterations observed in semagacestat-treated patients in the failed Phase-3 IDENTITY clinical trial (Doody et al., 2013) and that semagacestat, like Aβ42, acts as a high affinity competitor of substrates (Koch et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koch et al., 2023.

claim: The convergence of Aβ42 and tau at the synapse has been proposed to underlie synaptic dysfunction in AD.
source: The convergence of Aβ42 and tau at the synapse has been proposed to underlie synaptic dysfunction in AD (McInnes et al., 2018; Ittner et al., 2010; Roberson et al., 2007; Spires-Jones and Hyman, 2014), and recent assessment of APP-CTF levels in synaptosome-enriched fractions from healthy control, SAD, and FAD brains (temporal cortices) has shown that APP fragments concentrate at higher levels in the synapse in AD-affected than in control individuals (Ferrer-Raventós, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McInnes et al., 2018; Ittner et al., 2010; Roberson et al., 2007; Spires-Jones and Hyman, 2014; Ferrer-Raventós, 2023.

claim: APP fragments concentrate at higher levels in the synapse in AD-affected than in control individuals.
source: The convergence of Aβ42 and tau at the synapse has been proposed to underlie synaptic dysfunction in AD (McInnes et al., 2018; Ittner et al., 2010; Roberson et al., 2007; Spires-Jones and Hyman, 2014), and recent assessment of APP-CTF levels in synaptosome-enriched fractions from healthy control, SAD, and FAD brains (temporal cortices) has shown that APP fragments concentrate at higher levels in the synapse in AD-affected than in control individuals (Ferrer-Raventós, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ferrer-Raventós, 2023.

claim: The deposition of Aβ42 in plaques may be preceded by a critical increase in the levels of Aβ present in endosomes and the cyclical inhibition of γ-secretase activity.
source: In addition, we argue that the deposition of Aβ42 in plaques may be preceded by a critical increase in the levels of Aβ present in endosomes and the cyclical inhibition of γ-secretase activity that we propose.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed model.

claim: Reductions in γ-secretase activity may be a (transient) downstream consequence of increases in Aβ due to failed clearance, as represented by plaque deposition, contributing to AD pathogenesis.
source: Under this view, reductions in γ-secretase activity may be a (transient) downstream consequence of increases in Aβ due to failed clearance, as represented by plaque deposition, contributing to AD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed model.

claim: Direct quantification of γ-secretase activity in detergent-resistant fractions prepared from post-mortem brain samples of healthy controls and FAD-linked mutation carriers revealed similar overall γ-secretase activity levels.
source: In this regard, the direct quantification of γ-secretase activity in detergent-resistant fractions prepared from post-mortem brain samples of healthy controls and FAD-linked mutation carriers revealed similar overall γ-secretase activity levels, indicating that the wild-type (PSEN1 and PSEN2) γ-secretase complexes rescue any potential mutation-driven deficits in the processing of APP (Szaruga et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Szaruga et al., 2015.

claim: Wild-type (PSEN1 and PSEN2) γ-secretase complexes rescue any potential mutation-driven deficits in the processing of APP.
source: In this regard, the direct quantification of γ-secretase activity in detergent-resistant fractions prepared from post-mortem brain samples of healthy controls and FAD-linked mutation carriers revealed similar overall γ-secretase activity levels, indicating that the wild-type (PSEN1 and PSEN2) γ-secretase complexes rescue any potential mutation-driven deficits in the processing of APP (Szaruga et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of similar γ-secretase activity levels in FAD and control brains.

claim: APP-CTFs have been reported to accumulate in the FAD brain.
source: Yet APP-CTFs have been reported to accumulate in the FAD brain (Ferrer-Raventós, 2023; Pera et al., 2013) and the accumulation of APP-CTFs appears to correlate with Aβ levels at the synapse.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferrer-Raventós, 2023; Pera et al., 2013.

claim: The accumulation of APP-CTFs appears to correlate with Aβ levels at the synapse.
source: Yet APP-CTFs have been reported to accumulate in the FAD brain (Ferrer-Raventós, 2023; Pera et al., 2013) and the accumulation of APP-CTFs appears to correlate with Aβ levels at the synapse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reported accumulation of APP-CTFs and Aβ in FAD brains.

claim: The inhibition of γ-secretase by Aβ42 could resolve the apparent conflict between similar γ-secretase activity levels and APP-CTF accumulation in FAD brains.
source: The inhibition of γ-secretase by Aβ42 could resolve the apparent conflict.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed model.

claim: There is a mutation-driven enhanced generation of Aβ42 within the endolysosomal network in FAD.
source: Indeed, our data could reconcile these two seemingly exclusive hypotheses on the effects of FAD mutations in PSEN1 on the development of AD by noting that: (1) there is a mutation-driven enhanced generation of Aβ42 within the endolysosomal network; (2) that through both endosomal production and endocytosis Aβ42 increases to a level within the endolysosomal network sufficient to inhibit the γ-secretase complex; and (3) that in the case of FAD mutations the isolation of the γ-secretase releases Aβ42, thus restoring wild-type enzyme activity (Veugelen et al., 2016; Shen and Kelleher, 2007).
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed model and citations to Veugelen et al., 2016; Shen and Kelleher, 2007.

claim: Through both endosomal production and endocytosis Aβ42 increases to a level within the endolysosomal network sufficient to inhibit the γ-secretase complex.
source: Indeed, our data could reconcile these two seemingly exclusive hypotheses on the effects of FAD mutations in PSEN1 on the development of AD by noting that: (1) there is a mutation-driven enhanced generation of Aβ42 within the endolysosomal network; (2) that through both endosomal production and endocytosis Aβ42 increases to a level within the endolysosomal network sufficient to inhibit the γ-secretase complex; and (3) that in the case of FAD mutations the isolation of the γ-secretase releases Aβ42, thus restoring wild-type enzyme activity (Veugelen et al., 2016; Shen and Kelleher, 2007).
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed model.

claim: In the case of FAD mutations the isolation of the γ-secretase releases Aβ42, thus restoring wild-type enzyme activity.
source: Indeed, our data could reconcile these two seemingly exclusive hypotheses on the effects of FAD mutations in PSEN1 on the development of AD by noting that: (1) there is a mutation-driven enhanced generation of Aβ42 within the endolysosomal network; (2) that through both endosomal production and endocytosis Aβ42 increases to a level within the endolysosomal network sufficient to inhibit the γ-secretase complex; and (3) that in the case of FAD mutations the isolation of the γ-secretase releases Aβ42, thus restoring wild-type enzyme activity (Veugelen et al., 2016; Shen and Kelleher, 2007).
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed model and citations to Veugelen et al., 2016; Shen and Kelleher, 2007.

claim: Increased levels of endolysosomal Aβ42 with concurrent inhibition of γ-secretase may be responsible, at least in part, for the apparent γ-secretase loss-of-function phenotypes.
source: Thus, increased levels of endolysosomal Aβ42 with concurrent inhibition of γ-secretase may be responsible, at least in part, for the apparent γ-secretase loss-of-function phenotypes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proposed model.
